In [[mathematics]], {{nowrap|'''1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + ⋯'''}}, also written {{tmath|1= \textstyle \sum_{n=1}^{\infin} n^0 }}, {{tmath|1= \textstyle \sum_{n=1}^{\infin} 1^n }}, or simply {{tmath|1= \textstyle \sum_{n=1}^{\infin} 1 }}, is a [[divergent series]]. Nevertheless, it is sometimes imputed to have a value of {{tmath|1= -\tfrac{1}{2} }}, especially in physics. This value can be justified by certain mathematical methods for obtaining values from divergent series, including [[zeta function regularization]].

== As a divergent series ==
{{nowrap|1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + ⋯}} is a divergent series, meaning that its sequence of [[partial sum]]s does not converge to a [[limit of a sequence|limit]] in the [[real number]]s.

The sequence 1<sup>{{mvar|n}}</sup> can be thought of as a [[geometric series]] with the [[Geometric series#Common ratio r|common ratio]]&nbsp;1. For some other divergent geometric series, including [[Grandi's series]] with ratio&nbsp;−1, and the series 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + ⋯ with ratio 2, one can use the general solution for the sum of a geometric series with base 1 and ratio {{tmath|1= r }}, obtaining {{tmath|1= \tfrac{1}{1-r} }}, but this summation method fails for {{nowrap|1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + ⋯}}, producing a [[division by zero]].

Together with Grandi's series, this is one of two geometric series with [[rational number|rational]] ratio that diverges both for the real numbers and for all systems of [[p-adic number|{{mvar|p}}-adic numbers]].

In the context of the [[extended real number line]]
: <math>\sum_{n=1}^{\infin} 1 = +\infty \, ,</math>
since its sequence of partial sums increases [[monotonic function|monotonically]] without bound.

== Zeta function regularization ==
Where the sum of {{math|''n''<sup>0</sup>}} occurs in [[theoretical physics|physical]] applications, it may sometimes be interpreted by [[zeta function regularization]], as the value at {{math|1=''s'' = 0}} of the [[Riemann zeta function]]:
: <math>\zeta(s)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{1}{n^s}=\frac{1}{1-2^{1-s}}\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n^s}\,.</math>

The two formulas given above are not valid at zero however, but the [[analytic continuation]] is
: <math>
\zeta(s) = 2^s\pi^{s-1}\ \sin\left(\frac{\pi s}{2}\right)\ \Gamma(1-s)\ \zeta(1-s)
</math>

Using this one gets (given that {{math|Γ(1) {{=}} 1}}),
: <math>\zeta(0) = \frac{1}{\pi} \lim_{s \rightarrow 0} \ \sin\left(\frac{\pi s}{2}\right)\ \zeta(1-s) = \frac{1}{\pi} \lim_{s \rightarrow 0} \ \left( \frac{\pi s}{2} - \frac{\pi^3 s^3}{48} + ... \right)\ \left( -\frac{1}{s} + ... \right) = -\frac{1}{2}</math>
where the power series expansion for {{math|''ζ''(''s'')}} about {{math|1=''s'' = 1}} follows because {{math|''ζ''(''s'')}} has a simple pole of [[residue (complex analysis)|residue]] one there. In this sense, {{math|1=1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + ⋯ = ''ζ''(0) = −{{sfrac|1|2}}}}.

[[Emilio Elizalde]] presents a comment from others about the series, suggesting the centrality of the zeta function regularization of this series in physics:
{{blockquote|1=In a short period of less than a year, two distinguished physicists, [[Andrei Slavnov|A. Slavnov]] and [[Francisco José Ynduráin|F. Yndurain]], gave seminars in Barcelona, about different subjects. It was remarkable that, in both presentations, at some point the speaker addressed the audience with these words: '''As everybody knows'', {{nowrap|1=1 + 1 + 1 + ⋯ = −{{sfrac|1|2}}}}.' Implying maybe: ''If you do not know this, it is no use to continue listening.''<ref>Emphasis in original. {{cite encyclopedia |first=Emilio |last=Elizalde |chapter=Cosmology: Techniques and Applications |title=Proceedings of the II International Conference on Fundamental Interactions |year=2004 |arxiv=gr-qc/0409076|bibcode=2004gr.qc.....9076E }}</ref>}}
